extracted.intended_audience: NLP / computational linguistics researchers and practitioners working on automatic humor recognition or joke detection
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and extract textual features that distinguish humorous from non-humorous text (especially one-liners) and use them to build classifiers. The page summarizes feature categories, salient signals, and a short evaluation rubric for joke-like text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phonetic devices (alliteration, rhyme)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the joke use phonetic devices such as alliteration or rhyme?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sound matters: phonetic/stylistic features are surface, content-independent markers of 'joke-like' text and were found at least as important as content features. Count or detect chains of repeated initial or end sounds; presence of these devices increases likelihood of humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alliteration chains
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated initial sounds (chains of words beginning with the same sound).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alliteration is a phonetic/stylistic marker cited as predictive of joke-like text. Measure length/frequency of alliteration chains as a feature; useful as a surface cue independent of semantic content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhyme chains
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition of end sounds across words/phrases (rhyming patterns).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rhyme is another phonetic device indicative of humorous one-liners. Detect end-sound repetition or rhyming pairs/chains; use as a stylistic feature alongside alliteration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antonymy / script opposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence of antonymous or contrasting words (indicating script opposition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Antonymy serves as a surface marker of script opposition, a theorized cognitive mechanism in humor. Detect antonym pairs or contrasting semantic markers between parts of the text; supports the idea of a punchline flipping the expected script.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content-based vocabulary (bag-of-words / n-grams)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lexical items and n-grams characteristic of jokes versus non-jokes (bag-of-words models trained on joke corpora).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train bag-of-words or n-gram classifiers on jokes vs. non-jokes: certain words and collocations are strongly predictive. The paper found vocabulary biased toward specific topics (sex, violence, body humor, embarrassment). Use supervised learners (Naïve Bayes, SVM) on these features for classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human-centeredness
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the joke centers on humans or human relationships rather than things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jokes tend to be about people more than objects: pronouns, relational words, kinship terms, and body-part references are overrepresented. Measure presence/frequency of human-referent tokens as a predictive feature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative polarity / taboo / charged topics
rubrics_metrics.description: Bias toward negative words and taboo or charged topics (sex, violence, body humor, embarrassment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is a slight bias toward negative sentiment and a concentration of taboo topics in joke vocabularies. Flagging sex/violence/body/taboo lexicons can improve detection; be aware these topics dominate joke corpora used in the study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polarity contrast between setup and punch (sentiment flip)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the punchline flips sentiment/polarity relative to the setup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often the punchline in a joke reverses or contrasts the sentiment of the setup. Detect sentiment shifts between parts (clauses, sentences, or the two halves of a one-liner) as an indicator of humor; use sentiment analysis to capture polarity contrast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of supervised classifiers (Naïve Bayes, SVM) for evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply standard classifiers (Naïve Bayes, Support Vector Machines) trained on labeled joke vs. non-joke corpora to evaluate feature effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper uses classifiers trained on one-liner corpora versus proverbs/news to show feature importance and improvements over baselines. While not a linguistic feature, choice of model and training corpus is part of the practical rubric for building and evaluating humor-detection systems.
